newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Petronas, KIMB in focus.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Petronas, KIMB in focus.

text.p: Asian debt markets received some notable news overnight when Malaysian state oil company Petronas priced its global bond.
More big news was forthcoming late on Friday when the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development announced, as expected, that South Korea had been offered membership.

Membership in the OECD is good news for South Korean borrowers because loans to these entities would qualify for a 20 percent rather than 100 percent risk weighting under OECD rules, meaning that returns to lenders would be sharply higher.
Debt issues of the top-ranked Korean banks have enjoyed a bull run in the secondary market over the last few months on views an offer of membership was imminent.
On Friday, Korea International Merchant Bank launched a US$70 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue.
The three-year certificates pay a margin of 50 basis points over the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate and, with fees, an all-in return of 64 basis points.
WestLB, Cho Hung Bank and Commerz East Asia are arrangers.
Pricing is a couple of basis points wider than KIMB's previous issue, which was launched in July and paid an all-in return of 62 basis points for three-year paper.
Korean merchant bank paper has not fared as well in the secondary market as that of the higher rated commercial banks.
Elsewhere, the hugely successful three-tranche Petronas bond issue was raised to US$1.9 billion from US$1.5 billion at launch due to strong demand, especially from U.S. investors.
As expected, almost all of the US$500 million 30-year tranche placed in the U.S., where there is a large institutional investor base eager to take long-dated paper.
Steve Roberts, managing director at Salomon Brothers in Hong Kong, said about 35 percent of the US$800 million 10-year tranche placed in Europe and Asia while the rest was taken up by U.S. investors.
Of the US$600 million five-year tranche, 80 percent placed in Europe and 15 percent went to Asian accounts.
Petronas, which already has mature access to the U.S. market and benefits from name recognition in Asia, targetted European investors in this latest issue, Roberts said.

The Petronas 6.625 percent five-year bond was priced to yield 38 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries, the 7.125 percent 10-year bond was priced to yield 57 basis points over Treasuries and the 7.625 percent 30-year bond was priced to yield 84 basis points over the benchmark.
All three tranches priced toward the tighter end of their indicated spread range.
A few other tidbits emerged on Friday.
Deals on the outlook for launch next week include a US$80 million loan for Cosco Hong Kong, a US$50 million deal for South Korea's Kumho Bank and a US$50 million FRCD for the Philippines Allied Bank.
Bankers said Seoulbank is looking for arrangers for a US$150 million borrowing.
Indicative terms for Videocon's US$70 million seven-year floating rate note have been offered to the market by arranger Peregrine Fixed Income, bankers said.
The notes are expected to be priced at between 220 and 250 basis points over LIBOR and fees range from 50 to 100 basis points depending on commitment.
Peregrine is expected to price the US$100 million FRN for Bakrie Brothers next Tuesday.
The notes, which have a final maturity of three years but can be put or called after two, have an indicated price range of between 200 and 225 basis points over LIBOR.
